title: My Clinic — RCM Part A: Documentation & ICD-10 Coding That Gets Approved
description: Clinical documentation improvement for physicians: medical necessity, specific ICD-10 coding, avoiding defensive medicine and common rejection causes.

metadata.description: Clinical documentation improvement for physicians: medical necessity, specific ICD-10 coding, avoiding defensive medicine and common rejection causes.

objectives.description: Document a complete, medically necessary clinical picture.
Select a specific, covered ICD-10 code, using a provisional diagnosis when justified.
Avoid defensive medicine and unjustified early repetition of tests.
Classify rejection causes and apply coverage awareness.
Improve a weak consultation note so that it is clear, strong and defensible.

screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: The reviewer only has your note. Good documentation protects the patient, you and the clinic.
screens.media_alt: A reviewer sees only the written note, not the patient encounter.
screens.body_html:
SECTION 1 OF 6

“The payer doesn't see your patient. The payer sees your note.”

Clinical decision + documentation + coding = optimised payment.

Dr. Omar: “Nobody taught me documentation for insurance at medical school. My first month, a lot of my claims came back.”

Examples in this module teach documentation, not treatment. All notes and patients are fictional.

screens.title: Productive failure
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: This reflection is not scored. Choose the response that helps you set one intention for your next shift.
screens.prompt_html: What do you think is the #1 cause of rejections at My Clinic?
screens.reflection_html: Hold that thought — we'll check it later. This reflection is not scored.

screens.title: Always / Avoid
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: What always goes in, what never should.
screens.prompt_html:
SECTION 2 OF 6

Every service must be clinically justified. Open both tabs.

tabs.label: Always
tabs.body_html:
• Chief complaint and history of present illness (HPI)
  • Relevant clinical findings
  • Link the symptoms to the working diagnosis
  • Labs or imaging to support the diagnosis, when needed

tabs.label: Avoid
tabs.body_html:
• Vague or incomplete notes
  • A diagnosis with no clinical support
  • Copy-paste without clinical relevance
  • Stand-alone entries such as “fatigue only” or “body pain”

screens.title: Weak vs strong
screens.notes: Companion: Noor, char-noor-avatar-neutral + tip card, L3 tip card (rendered as the companion-tip paragraph; image_compare has no media slot for the avatar). Speaker: Noor. Alt text — before: 'Weak note: patient given IV fluids.' after: 'Strong note: dehydration signs, IV fluids for stabilisation.' Clinical example ⚠ Draft — pending B10.
screens.narration_text: Noor: Same patient, same fluids. One note gets paid.
screens.prompt_html:
Drag the slider to compare two notes for the same fictional patient and the same treatment.

Noor's tip: Nurses' notes count too. The vital signs we record are what justify the order.

Teaching example ⚠ Draft — pending B10.
screens.after_label: Strong: “Dehydration signs (HR 112, dry mucosa) — IV fluids started for stabilisation.”
screens.caption: Same treatment, different outcome: only the second note answers the reviewer's question, “Why was this done?”

screens.title: The full clinical picture
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Put the steps in the order you would follow at work, then read the feedback.
screens.prompt_html: Put the parts of a complete consultation note in order, from first to last.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Good documentation tells a story, not just a diagnosis: the complaint and history lead to findings, the findings support the assessment, and the plan says how long and what happens next.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not yet. Good documentation tells a story, not just a diagnosis. Start with why the patient came, then the history, then what you found. The assessment follows from the findings, and the plan, with its duration and follow-up, comes last.

screens.title: Medical necessity
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Decide as you would on shift, then read the feedback.

options.feedback_html: “Routine” gives no indication. The reviewer asks why was this done? and finds no answer.
A single vague symptom on its own is listed under Avoid. It doesn't explain why a CBC was needed.

options.text_html: “Fatigue for 6 weeks, pallor, menorrhagia — rule out anaemia.”
options.feedback_html: Yes. Duration, a finding and a history point to a clear suspicion, and the test is linked to it.
A request is not an indication. Give patients what they need, not only what they ask for.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. The reviewer asks one question: why was this done? Duration, pallor and menorrhagia, linked to “rule out anaemia”, answer it.
feedback.incorrect_html: The reviewer asks: why was this done? Only the note with a duration, a finding and a linked suspicion (fatigue for 6 weeks, pallor, menorrhagia — rule out anaemia) answers that.

screens.title: Coding is clinical translation
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Coding is clinical translation. Specific codes get accepted.

blocks.html:
SECTION 3 OF 6

Coding is not administrative. It's clinical translation.

  • Primary diagnosis = the main condition treated
  • Secondary diagnoses = show the complexity
  • Specific code = higher acceptance; it justifies the medicines and services
  • #1 rejection cause: non-specific coding of symptoms

Avoid: the symptom codeReach: the supported diagnosis
Fever (R50)Identify the cause
Cough (R05)Identify the cause
Vomiting (R11)Gastroenteritis (K52)
Sore throatAcute tonsillitis (J03)
HeadacheHypertension (I10), when clinically supported

Codes and titles ⚠ Draft — pending B4. Don't stop at the symptom: reach the most supported clinical diagnosis.

screens.title: Symptom → supported diagnosis
screens.notes: All codes and titles ⚠ Draft — pending B4 (ICD-10 edition and code validation by the Coding lead). Gastroenteritis uses the source's K52; B4 notes it may be A09 (infectious).
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Match each item to the person or step that owns it, then read the feedback.
screens.prompt_html:
Match each presentation to the most specific supported diagnosis.

Codes and titles ⚠ Draft — pending B4 (ICD-10 edition and coder validation).

pairs.left_html: Vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days, dry mucosa

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Don't stop at the symptom. Each presentation has findings that support a specific diagnosis, and the specific code is what gets accepted. Codes ⚠ Draft — pending B4.
feedback.incorrect_html: Don't stop at the symptom. Look for the finding that points to the diagnosis: exudate for tonsillitis, two raised readings for hypertension, HbA1c for diabetes, and dehydration with vomiting and diarrhoea for gastroenteritis. Codes ⚠ Draft — pending B4.

screens.title: Provisional diagnosis
screens.notes: Fictional teaching case; clinical example and code ⚠ Draft — pending B10 / B4.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Follow the example one step at a time, then identify why the next step makes sense.
screens.intro_html: Fictional case. An adult has had fever for 3 days, with dysuria and suprapubic pain. You order investigations before the diagnosis is confirmed. Golden tip: a provisional diagnosis is allowed when it is clinically justified.

steps.action_html: Record the presentation: fever for 3 days, dysuria, suprapubic pain, and your examination findings.
steps.rationale_html: The reviewer only sees the note. The findings show why investigations follow.
Each test is linked to a documented suspicion, so it is medically necessary.

steps.action_html: Document a provisional diagnosis linked to the findings, e.g. suspected lower urinary tract infection. Code ⚠ Draft — pending B4.
steps.rationale_html: Honest about uncertainty, still specific. “Fever” alone is a non-specific symptom code, the top cause of rejection.

steps.action_html: When the results return, confirm or change the diagnosis and update the plan.
steps.rationale_html: The final diagnosis follows the evidence, and the record shows your reasoning from start to finish.

screens.self_explanation_prompt_html: Why is a provisional diagnosis better than “fever” here? Write a sentence for yourself. This is not scored.

screens.title: Covered or not as primary?
screens.notes: Uncovered list from the source; codes ⚠ Draft — pending B4. Obesity BMI > 40 with surgical referral rule ⚠ Draft — pending B5. BMI nuance explained only in feedback, as the card says.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Place each item where it belongs, then read the feedback.
screens.prompt_html: Sort each diagnosis: avoid it as the primary diagnosis, or covered when clinically supported? Codes ⚠ Draft — pending B4; coverage per the current table of benefits.

items.text_html: Obesity with BMI 42, referred for bariatric surgery ⚠ Draft — pending B5

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Link to a covered condition when it truly exists, or don't use it as the main diagnosis. Obesity is the nuance: uncovered for medical treatment, but covered with BMI above 40 and a surgical referral ⚠ Draft — pending B5.
feedback.incorrect_html: Link to a covered condition when it truly exists, or don't use it as the main diagnosis. Acne, hair loss, seborrhoeic dermatitis, infertility, general check-ups and obesity at BMI 31 are commonly uncovered as primary. Obesity at BMI 42 with a surgical referral is the exception ⚠ Draft — pending B5.

screens.title: More tests ≠ better care
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Defensive medicine feels safe but gets rejected. Follow work-up protocols, document deviations.

blocks.html:
SECTION 4 OF 6

Defensive medicine feels safe, but it increases rejections.

  • Follow initial work-up protocols
  • No supplements without an indication; combined supplements count as defensive medicine ⚠ Draft — pending B8
  • Repeat tests only at evidence-based intervals
  • If you deviate, document why

TestRepeat no earlier than
Vitamin DThe payer-approved interval ⚠ Draft — pending B2
HbA1cAbout 3 months (90 days) ⚠ Draft — pending B3

Unjustified repetition leads to rejection. A documented clinical reason is what justifies an early repeat.

screens.title: Joint-pain case
screens.notes: Companion: Dr. Omar, char-omar-avatar-thinking → char-omar-avatar-happy / char-omar-avatar-concern, L5 avatar (host row on the intro; feedback avatar only, never over the choices). Speaker: Omar. Defensive-medicine scenario from the source script; clinical example ⚠ Draft — pending B10. pass_score 2 (both best).
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Play the situation through and decide, then read the feedback.
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-omar-avatar-neutral}}Dr. Omar · Family physician

Fictional case. A 45-year-old patient comes to you with pain in several joints. Two decisions: what to order, and what changes when there is a history.

feedback.correct_html: Both best choices. Start with the initial work-up; when a specialist diagnosis exists, document it and the full panel is justified in one request. ⚠ Draft — pending B10
feedback.incorrect_html: More tests are not better care. Follow the initial work-up first, and document the history or specialist diagnosis that justifies a fuller panel. ⚠ Draft — pending B10

nodes.prompt_html: First visit. Multi-joint pain, no previous history, no earlier work-up. What do you order?

choices.text_html: Everything at once: CRP, ESR, anti-DNA, anti-Ro, anti-La.
choices.feedback_html: This is the script's example of defensive medicine: specific antibody tests requested all at once, with nothing documented to justify them, risk rejection as early and unjustified. ⚠ Draft — pending B10

choices.text_html: The initial work-up, CRP and ESR, with the history and examination findings documented.
choices.feedback_html: Best choice. Follow the initial work-up protocol first. Specific tests follow when the results and findings justify them. ⚠ Draft — pending B10

choices.text_html: No tests; write “joint pain” and review later.
choices.feedback_html: “Joint pain” on its own is a vague symptom note, and it skips the initial work-up the patient needs. Document the findings and start the protocol.

nodes.prompt_html: Now imagine the same patient already has rheumatoid arthritis, diagnosed by a rheumatologist elsewhere. What do you do?

choices.text_html: Document the history and the specialist's diagnosis, then request the full panel in one request.
choices.feedback_html: Best choice. As the script says: mention the past history or the specialist's diagnosis, and the full lab panel can be requested in one request. ⚠ Draft — pending B10

choices.text_html: Order the full panel, but leave the earlier diagnosis out of the note.
choices.feedback_html: The panel may be clinically right, but the reviewer can't see why. Without the documented history it looks like the first-visit request and risks rejection.

choices.text_html: Split the tests across several visits so that no single request looks excessive.
choices.feedback_html: Splitting delays care and multiplies requests. The documented specialist diagnosis is what justifies the full panel in one request.

screens.title: Timing
screens.notes: HbA1c repeat interval shown as the draft value 'about 3 months (90 days)' from the source note ⚠ Draft — pending B3.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Decide as you would on shift, then read the feedback.
screens.prompt_html: Your fictional patient with diabetes had an HbA1c 6 weeks ago. He asks for another one today. What is the best action?

options.text_html: Repeat it today because the patient asked.
options.feedback_html: A request is not a clinical reason. Early repetition with no documented reason is rejected.

options.text_html: Don't repeat it yet unless there is a documented clinical reason; plan the next test at the approved interval (about 3 months / 90 days ⚠ Draft — pending B3).
options.feedback_html: Yes. Follow the evidence-based interval, and document the reason if you ever need to repeat early. Interval ⚠ Draft — pending B3.

options.text_html: Repeat it under a general check-up code.
options.feedback_html: A general check-up is commonly uncovered as primary, and it doesn't make an early repeat justified.

options.text_html: Repeat it and explain only if the claim is rejected.
options.feedback_html: The reviewer decides from the note as it stands. Justification has to be documented at the time.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Unjustified repetition leads to rejection. Wait for the approved interval (about 3 months ⚠ Draft — pending B3) unless you document a clinical reason.
feedback.incorrect_html: Six weeks is earlier than the approved interval (about 3 months ⚠ Draft — pending B3). Without a documented clinical reason, an early repeat is likely to be rejected.

screens.title: Supplements
screens.notes: 'Combined supplements are treated as defensive medicine' ⚠ Draft — pending B8 (payer rule vs internal guidance).
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Decide as you would on shift, then read the feedback.
screens.prompt_html:
Prescribing a combined multivitamin “for general wellness”, with no documented deficiency, is likely to be rejected.

⚠ Draft — pending B8

feedback.correct_html: Right. Supplements need a documented indication. Combined supplements are treated as defensive medicine ⚠ Draft — pending B8.
feedback.incorrect_html: It is likely to be rejected: there's no documented indication. Combined supplements are treated as defensive medicine ⚠ Draft — pending B8.

screens.title: Four causes
screens.notes: Four items from the card plus four built from the source script ('+ 4 more'). 'Non-specific coding of symptoms' as the single biggest cause comes from the script's ICD-10 section. Codes ⚠ Draft — pending B4.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Let's check your earlier guess. Place each item where it belongs, then read the feedback.
screens.prompt_html: Each fictional rejection note has one main cause. Place it under the right cause.

items.text_html: “Vitamin D, B12 and multivitamin; no deficiency documented.”
“Antibiotic billed for a viral URTI code.”
“Knee MRI billed under a headache diagnosis.”

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Those are the four common causes. Now check your guess from the start of the module: the single biggest cause is a non-specific diagnosis, coding the symptom instead of the supported diagnosis.
feedback.incorrect_html: Ask what the reviewer could not find: a reason (justification), a specific diagnosis, the findings or plan (incomplete), or a treatment that fits the diagnosis (mismatch). And your earlier guess? The single biggest cause is a non-specific diagnosis.

screens.title: Coverage changes
screens.notes: Regulator name shown as the D4 recommended draft (current official English name and acronym): Council of Health Insurance (CHI) ⚠ Draft — pending D4 / B1. Mental-health sub-limit (B7) deliberately not shown; covered in module 06.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Coverage changes often. Part B covers what's new.

blocks.html:
SECTION 5 OF 6

Insurance is not static. Under the Council of Health Insurance (CHI) ⚠ Draft — pending D4, benefits are added and amended often.

  • Know what is covered and what is not
  • Adapt your documentation to the coverage conditions
  • Partial coverage does not mean full approval

“If you don't document it properly, it won't be covered — even if it's clinically correct.”

The same service may be accepted or rejected depending on its indication and how it is documented: record the severity, the duration and the impact on the patient.

Next: RCM Part B covers the new essential benefits package (EBP).

screens.title: Coverage check
screens.notes: PCOS vs menopause hormonal assessment ⚠ Draft — pending B6 (links to module 06).
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Decide as you would on shift, then read the feedback.
screens.prompt_html: Which hormonal assessment is likely to be approved? ⚠ Draft — pending B6

options.text_html: Hormonal assessment for menopausal symptoms, with the symptoms, severity and duration documented.
options.feedback_html: Yes. In the source's example, assessment for menopausal conditions is approved. ⚠ Draft — pending B6

options.text_html: Hormonal work-up for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
options.feedback_html: In the source's example, a PCOS hormonal assessment is rejected as uncovered. ⚠ Draft — pending B6

options.text_html: Both are approved the same way, whatever the note says.
options.feedback_html: The same service can be accepted or rejected depending on the indication and the documentation.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. The same service can be accepted or rejected depending on indication and documentation. ⚠ Draft — pending B6
feedback.incorrect_html: The same service can be accepted or rejected depending on indication and documentation. Here the menopausal indication is covered and the PCOS work-up is not. ⚠ Draft — pending B6

screens.title: Fix the note
screens.notes: Companions: Dr. Omar char-omar-avatar (host, avatar row on the intro); Noor char-noor-tip (hints, text in the hint ladder). L5. Speakers: Omar + Noor (omar-1, noor-1). Notes rcma-img-notes-1..3 are HTML text inside each node. case_sim, 3 notes, +1 per best rewrite, pass_score 2, 1 hint per note (cost 0), no lives, no timer. Depends on B8 (combined supplements), B2 (vitamin D interval), B4 (codes), B10 (clinical examples), G4 (single capstone for rcma-o5). The card's 'B12' dependency is the vitamin, not a Phase 0 row.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Three notes, your pen. Play the round, then read the feedback. Noor: That is the habit we want from every new colleague.
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-omar-avatar-neutral}}Dr. Omar · Family physician

Three weak notes, written by a fictional colleague. For each one, choose the rewrite a reviewer would approve. One point per best rewrite; you need 2 of 3. Noor has one hint for each note. No lives, no timer.

hints.text: Noor, note 1: A reviewer looks for the evidence behind each supplement. One indicated supplement beats three hopeful ones.
Noor, note 2: Ask which finding justifies an antibiotic. A symptom code can't.
Noor, note 3: Is there a covered condition this visit is actually managing?

nodes.content_html:
Note 1 of 3

Fictional note

“Body pain. Vit D + B12 + multivitamin.”

Choose the best rewrite.

choices.text_html: “Generalised aches and fatigue for 3 months; limited sun exposure. Vitamin D level low (deficient). Plan: vitamin D replacement only; recheck at the approved interval ⚠ Draft — pending B2; review in clinic.”
choices.feedback_html: Best rewrite. Findings, evidence of the deficiency, one indicated supplement and a follow-up. ⚠ Draft — pending B2 · ⚠ Draft — pending B10

choices.text_html: “Body pain and fatigue. Vitamin D, B12 and multivitamin. Review as needed.”
choices.feedback_html: Still vague, and still combined supplements with no documented deficiency, treated as defensive medicine ⚠ Draft — pending B8.

choices.text_html: “Patient requests vitamins for energy. Multivitamin prescribed as requested.”
choices.feedback_html: A request is not an indication. Give patients what they need, not only what they ask for.

nodes.content_html:
Note 2 of 3

Fictional note

“Cough. Augmentin.”

Choose the best rewrite.

choices.feedback_html: A symptom code, the top cause of rejection, and nothing that justifies an antibiotic. Code ⚠ Draft — pending B4

choices.text_html: “Productive cough for 6 days, fever 38.6 °C, crackles at the right base; chest X-ray shows right lower-lobe consolidation. Assessment: community-acquired pneumonia ⚠ Draft — pending B4. Plan: amoxicillin–clavulanate for a documented duration; review in 48 hours.”
choices.feedback_html: Best rewrite. A specific diagnosis, and findings that justify the antibiotic, with duration and follow-up. Code ⚠ Draft — pending B4 · ⚠ Draft — pending B10

choices.text_html: “Viral upper respiratory tract infection. Augmentin for 7 days.”
choices.feedback_html: The diagnosis and the treatment don't match: an antibiotic billed for a viral URTI is rejected.

nodes.content_html:
Note 3 of 3

Fictional note

“Check-up. Full labs.”

Choose the best rewrite.

choices.text_html: “General check-up ⚠ Draft — pending B4 as the primary diagnosis. CBC, lipids, TSH, vitamin D, liver and renal function.”
choices.feedback_html: General check-up codes are commonly uncovered as primary, and the long list of tests has no indication.
“Fatigue only” is a vague entry, and “full labs” justifies none of the tests.

choices.text_html: “Follow-up of known type 2 diabetes (E11) ⚠ Draft — pending B4; last HbA1c 7 months ago. Ordered: HbA1c, renal function and lipid profile for diabetes monitoring. Other screening requested by the patient is not claimed under this diagnosis.”
choices.feedback_html: Best rewrite. The visit is linked to the covered condition it actually manages, each test fits it, and anything without a covered indication is billed the way your RCM team directs rather than claimed.

nodes.content_html:
Debrief: clear, strong, defensible

  1. Be specific; avoid uncovered ICD-10 codes and combined supplements.
  2. Full medical data and a management plan with duration and expected outcome.
  3. Justify every service and medicine with a specific code; write a provisional diagnosis if needed.
  4. Think like a clinician and a reviewer.
  5. If you don't follow a protocol, document why.
  6. Make it clear, strong and defensible.

choices.text_html: Close the case and see your score.
choices.feedback_html: Your score counts one point for each best rewrite. You need 2 of 3 to pass.

feedback.correct_html: Well fixed. Your rewrites give the reviewer the findings, the specific diagnosis and the plan. That's the habit we want from every colleague.
feedback.incorrect_html: Some rewrites still leave the reviewer asking why was this done? Read the feedback for each note, use Noor's hints, and try again.

screens.title: Results
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Your results are organised by objective. Notice where you were confident, then revisit any section that needs another practical try.
screens.body_html: Passing score: 80% (80 / 100 points). Sections below 70% show what to revisit.

screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: You can now use these key actions in your role. Keep the practical rule close, ask when you are unsure, and carry the next step into your shift. Take one clear next action with you.
screens.body_html:
Clear, strong, defensible: the checklist to keep at your desk

  • ✔ Be specific; avoid uncovered codes and combined supplements.
  • ✔ Full data, and a plan with duration and expected outcome.
  • ✔ Justify every service with a specific code; use a provisional diagnosis if needed.
  • ✔ Think like a clinician and a reviewer.
  • ✔ If you skip a protocol, document why.
  • ✔ Clear, strong, defensible.

Next: RCM Part B. Printable desk checklist: pending production (rcma-pdf-checklist).
